summary: Front light of the Swash Channel range on Staten Island: 1855 wooden tower, moved in 1891, replaced in 1939, range discontinued in 1964.

structures.note: About 55 ft (17 m) tall; the USLHS record gives 1856 for the station; moved about 265 ft north-east in 1891; torn down in 1939 (Lighthouse Friends; Rowlett; LHB 1891 entry).
Replaced the wooden tower; 65 ft (20 m) per Lighthouse Friends and Rowlett, 60 ft above water and 55 ft to lantern centre per USLHS; unpainted per Rowlett; carried an aviation beacon.

access.note: Owned by the National Park Service and part of Gateway National Recreation Area; grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends; Rowlett). Located in Miller Field, a former Army air field.

events.note: Board contract dated 11 June 1855 for six range beacons, $19,124 for the whole, works due 25 October 1855 (Board's 1855 report as quoted by Lighthouse Friends)
Tower began operating in 1855 (Lighthouse Friends); USLHS and Rowlett date the station to 1856
Third-order range lens (Lighthouse Friends); USLHS gives 1856 as the year the original lens was installed
Tower moved about 265 ft north-east to mark the axis of the Swash Channel, 30 June 1891 (Lighthouse Board); Lighthouse Friends gives 250 ft
Discontinued as a war measure on 28 April 1898, with the Swash Channel range listed among lights extinguished (Lighthouse Board; The Sun reported the order on 30 April)
Edward B. Burdge appointed; began at Elm Tree on 14 April 1906, after Jacob C. Swaim's death on 14 February 1906 (Lighthouse Friends)
Miller Airfield built next to the light, November 1919, on the former William H. Vanderbilt farm (Lighthouse Friends)
Elm Tree and New Dorp beacons changed from incandescent oil vapor to electric incandescent (Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1924)
Old wooden tower torn down; light moved to a 65 ft concrete tower that also carried an aviation beacon, maintained by the City of New York Armory Board (Lighthouse Friends; Rowlett)

16 December 1960: TWA and United Airlines aircraft collided above Miller Field, next to the light; the TWA wreckage fell at Miller Field, the United jet crashed in Brooklyn (Lighthouse Friends). Sources read do not say the light was involved
Range discontinued when its alignment was changed; channel markers replaced it (USLHS; Rowlett; Lighthouse Friends)
Land turned over to the National Park Service (Lighthouse Friends)

notes_for_editor: Moderate evidence: official Board entries (1891 move, 1898 war measure), one contemporary newspaper page (The Sun, 30 April 1898), the USLHS roster, Rowlett and Lighthouse Friends. No storms or shipwrecks at the station were found. Checked 2026-10-28. Disagreements: (1) first lit: Lighthouse Friends says the tower began operating in 1855 (the contract ran to 25 October 1855); USLHS and Rowlett give 1856 as the station's establishment and USLHS gives 1856 as the original lens year; the story gives both. (2) 1891 move: the Board's entry, read on the page image (scan p. 20, printed p. 13), says 'Moved about 265 feet N.E. 1/2 E. to mark the axis of the Swash Channel, June 30, 1891'; Lighthouse Friends says 250 feet; the story uses the Board's figure and says so. (3) Height of the 1939 tower: 65 ft (Lighthouse Friends, Rowlett: 'square cylindrical concrete tower') against 55 ft to lantern centre and 60 ft above water (USLHS); the story gives 65 ft and 60 ft above water. (4) Date of the 1898 war-time discontinuance: the Board's entry gives 28 April; The Sun (30 April) reports an order issued 'yesterday' (29 April); the story says so. (5) Height of light: the record's focal_height_m 18.3 follows USLHS '60 feet above water'; Lighthouse Friends gives 'a height of sixty-two feet above sea level' (about 18.9 m). Not resolved in the record. (6) Location: Lighthouse Friends' text says 'south side of the island'; its map text says 'eastern shore' and Rowlett says 'southeast end of New Dorp Avenue ... in Miller Field'. The story uses 'south side ... near the shore'. (7) Rowlett's 'Swash Channel Range Front (3?)' at Oakwood Beach (1939, active) is a different light, not this station; do not conflate the names. (8) Lighthouse Friends quotes the Board's 1855 report and a 1924 interview; both are second-hand here (footnote 1). The 1924 interview is quoted only as Lighthouse Friends gives it. (9) The 1899-volume item 371 (Elm Tree, New York Bay) was read in the corpus text; the 1924-29 Bulletin index entry (p. 137) was cited as an index entry only, not read in the body volume. (10) Chronicling America searches for Swaim (1906) returned nothing; the 1906 keeper change rests on Lighthouse Friends and the USLHS roster. Lighthouse Friends calls the widow 'Sara'; the roster prints 'Sara Ann Swaim'. (11) The 1960 collision is in Lighthouse Friends only; the sources read do not tie the light to it, and the victims are not named. (12) The Sun order's 'lower bay' list is quoted from the newspaper; the story says the paper described the lights 'left burning' rather than quoting that phrase. (13) Wikipedia was read for leads only and is not cited.
